item.content:encoded:
When Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin used the term “conscious uncoupling” to describe their separation in 2014, the phrase ended up going viral at the time, taking the internet by storm.
And now, we finally have its backstory.
Paltrow, 53, opened up about the term during a recent episode of podcast “Friends Keep Secrets.” It turns out, her introduction to the phrase came from a therapist that she and Martin had at the time.
“Chris and I had this therapist that was really brilliant, and he sort of introduced us to the concept,” Paltrow told hosts Benny Blanco, Lil Dicky and his wife Kristin Batalucco during the Sept. 8 episode. “We just made a commitment to really put the kids first, and so what that meant was to stay a family, even though we weren’t a couple.”
Paltrow — who is currently married to writer and director Brad Falchuk, 55 — shares two children with Martin, 49. The two announced the news of the divorce through a statement on her Goop website.
“We are parents first and foremost, to two incredibly wonderful children and we ask for their and our space and privacy to be respected at this difficult time,” Paltrow and Martin wrote in the statement. “We have always conducted our relationship privately, and we hope that as we consciously uncouple and coparent, we will be able to continue in the same manner.”
Paltrow told the podcast that when she and Martin decided to get divorced, she turned to friends who came from divorced households for guidance.
“I said, ‘Tell me, what was the worst thing? What do you feel you have scars from to this day?’” Paltrow recounted. “They said the worst part was ... ‘My dad used to drop me off at the end of the driveway.’ ‘It was so tense at my birthday parties.’ ‘They never ate dinner in the same room until my college graduation, and it caused me so much pain.’”
She added that she and Martin sought to “circumvent all of that awful stuff.” Paltrow also shared one particular trying moment during the divorce in which she had to put the conscious uncoupling philosophy to work. She explained that when the family moved to Los Angeles early on in the separation, they continued to have brunch together every Sunday. One particular brunch date proved difficult.
“Chris and I were upset with each other about something – I can’t even remember what it is — and I was like, ‘This might go really off the rails,’” she recalled. “It was getting tense, and we looked at each other. We went outside on the front porch, and we’re like, ‘Let’s just not.’”
She said that the two ended up embracing.
“We just hugged,” she said. “We like fist-bumped and then we went to brunch.”
Paltrow, to be clear, did not invent the term “conscious uncoupling.” The tactic, believed to be coined by late marriage and family therapist Katherine Woodward Thomas, has long existed with therapists and counselors encouraging the mindset as part of the final stage of marriage counseling after a decision to divorce is made.
Life coach Jeanne Byrd Romero previously told TODAY.com that conscious uncoupling is a method that can help the parties heal.
“It’s really a way of moving out of blame and shame so people can transform the experience into healing and peace,” Romero said. “It can be done with just one of the partners are the couple.”

item.content:encoded:
Gwyneth Paltrow unveils why she called Chris Martin divorce 'conscious uncoupling'
Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin welcomed two kids, daughter Apple and son Moses
Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin planned to "stay a family" after they parted ways.
The actress and the Coldplay frontman caused a stir back in 2014 when they first described their divorce as "conscious uncoupling.”
Now, the Marty Supreme star has described why they used the term and how they wanted to separate as smoothly as possible for their kids, daughter Apple Martin and son Moses.
“We really sat down and thought, like, is there a way that we could do this?" she said on the Friends Keep Secrets podcast.
She continued, “I talked to all my friends who came from a divorced household and I said, ‘Tell me what was the worst thing? Like, what do you feel you have scars from to this day?’”
Gwyneth admitted she was shocked to discover the problem was not the divorce but the challenges kids face growing up amid friction between parents.
The mom of two noted, “They said the worst part was like my parents, you know, my dad used to drop me off at the end of the driveway. Like it was so tense at my birthday parties, you know, they never ate dinner in the same room until my college graduation, and it caused me so much pain. So I was like, how could we not do that?”
So Gwyneth wanted her kids to grow up in a situation where “you’re all having dinner at the same table” no matter what.
She recalled, “So Chris and I had this therapist that was really brilliant, and he sort of introduced us to the concept and we just made a commitment to really put the kids first and so what that meant was to stay a family even though we weren’t a couple."
It is pertinent to mention that Gwyneth is now married to Brad Falchuk

item.content:encoded:
Frankie Muniz isn’t racing away from his struggles.
The Malcolm in the Middle actor got candid about what he’s been going through over the last six weeks, admitting his life has felt like “a nightmare I’m praying to wake up from.”
“Everything felt heavy, unclear, and like it was falling apart at the same time,” Muniz posted on X Sept. 18. “I wouldn’t wish this season on anyone.”
The admission comes over two months after he and wife Paige Price—with whom he shares 5-year-old son Mauz Mosley Muniz—announced their divorce after six years of marriage.
Still, there is a silver lining for the 40-year-old, as he explained, “The unexpected gift in the middle of it is that I’ve had nowhere to hide. I’ve had time to sit with myself, do real self-reflection, and finally see the areas of my life that need work if I want to become a better version of me. Not the polished version I show the world...the actual one.”
Muniz said he recently read that "sometimes hitting rock bottom is the thing that wakes you up" and becomes a catalyst to force “the changes you needed to make all along so you can live the best life possible.”
And that idea stayed with the race car driver, who imagined in five years time he will “look back at this exact low point and feel grateful for it,” especially because getting to a better place in his life necessitated going through the difficulty.
“This isn’t the end of the story. It’s the part where I start doing the work...the uncomfortable, unglamorous, necessary work. I’m choosing to treat this season as the foundation, not the finish line,” Muniz wrote. “If you’re in a low place right now too, you’re not broken. You’re being rebuilt. Let's keep going!”
In recent weeks, Muniz has been open about the difficult time he’s been facing, posting on X Aug. 26, “Am I naive to say that I didn't know that having a broken heart actually meant your heart physically aches. I'd rather break my back again.”
On Sept. 1 he wrote, “Struggling,” and a few days later on Sept. 6 shared two photos of himself as a child, captioning the pictures, “Sometimes I wish I could go back to this.”
